text: TP53 (tumour protein p53, UniProt P04637) is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer, with mutations found in approximately 50% of all tumour types. It functions as a transcription factor and tumour suppressor, activating genes involved in cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, senescence, and DNA repair in response to cellular stress. The protein forms tetramers and binds specific DNA response elements to regulate target gene expression. Under normal conditions, TP53 is kept at low levels through MDM2-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. DNA damage, oncogene activation, and hypoxia stabilise TP53 by disrupting MDM2 binding. Loss-of-function mutations in TP53 allow damaged cells to proliferate unchecked, contributing to tumourigenesis. Gain-of-function mutations can confer oncogenic properties beyond simple loss of tumour suppression. TP53 mutations are associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a hereditary cancer predisposition disorder.

BRCA1 (breast cancer type 1 susceptibility protein, UniProt P38398) is a tumour suppressor involved in DNA double-strand break repair via homologous recombination. It forms a heterodimer with BARD1 and interacts with BRCA2 and RAD51 to coordinate repair at stalled replication forks. BRCA1 also has roles in transcriptional regulation, centrosome duplication, and ubiquitin ligase activity through its RING domain. Germline pathogenic variants in BRCA1 confer a lifetime breast cancer risk of approximately 60-70% and ovarian cancer risk of 40-50%. BRCA1-associated cancers are frequently triple-negative (ER-, PR-, HER2-). BRCA1-deficient tumours are sensitive to PARP inhibitors (synthetic lethality) and platinum-based chemotherapy. Pathogenic variants are enriched in Ashkenazi Jewish populations. PALB2 acts as a bridging factor between BRCA1 and BRCA2, and PALB2 variants similarly elevate breast and ovarian cancer risk.

BRCA2 (breast cancer type 2 susceptibility protein, UniProt P51587) is a key mediator of homologous recombination repair. It directly binds RAD51 via BRC repeats and loads RAD51 onto single-stranded DNA at double-strand break sites, enabling strand invasion and template-directed repair. Unlike BRCA1, BRCA2 has no enzymatic activity — its function is structural, organising the RAD51 filament. Germline pathogenic variants in BRCA2 confer a lifetime breast cancer risk of approximately 45-55% and ovarian cancer risk of 10-20%. BRCA2 variants are also associated with elevated risk of pancreatic, prostate, and male breast cancer. Biallelic BRCA2 mutations cause Fanconi anaemia complementation group D1, a severe developmental disorder with extreme cancer predisposition. BRCA2-deficient cells are sensitive to PARP inhibitors. BRCA1 and BRCA2 interact via PALB2, forming a complex essential for efficient homologous recombination.

EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor, UniProt P00533) is a receptor tyrosine kinase of the ErbB family that controls cell proliferation, survival, and differentiation. Ligand binding (EGF, TGF-α) triggers receptor dimerisation, autophosphorylation, and downstream activation of RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT, and STAT3 pathways. EGFR is overexpressed or mutated in multiple cancer types. Activating mutations in exons 19 (deletions) and 21 (L858R substitution) are the most common oncogenic alterations in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and predict sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (gefitinib, erlotinib, osimertinib). The T790M gatekeeper mutation confers resistance to first- and second-generation inhibitors. EGFR amplification occurs in glioblastoma (often with the EGFRvIII deletion variant) and colorectal cancer. In colorectal cancer, KRAS mutations downstream of EGFR predict non-response to anti-EGFR antibodies (cetuximab, panitumumab).

KRAS (Kirsten RAS, UniProt P01116) is a small GTPase that cycles between active GTP-bound and inactive GDP-bound states, relaying proliferative signals from receptor tyrosine kinases to downstream effectors including RAF-MEK-ERK and PI3K-AKT. KRAS is the most frequently mutated oncogene in human cancer. Hotspot mutations at codons 12 and 13 (G12D, G12V, G12C, G13D) impair GTPase activity, locking KRAS in the active GTP-bound state. KRAS mutations are found in ~90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas, ~40% of colorectal cancers, and ~30% of lung adenocarcinomas. KRAS-mutant cancers are traditionally refractory to direct targeting; however, the G12C-specific covalent inhibitor sotorasib received FDA approval in 2021, establishing direct KRAS inhibition as clinically viable. KRAS mutations predict non-response to anti-EGFR therapies in colorectal cancer and are used as a negative predictive biomarker.

ATM (ataxia telangiectasia mutated, UniProt Q13315) is a serine/threonine kinase and master regulator of the DNA damage response. Upon detection of DNA double-strand breaks, ATM is activated by autophosphorylation and phosphorylates hundreds of substrates including H2AX, CHK2, BRCA1, and p53 to initiate cell cycle checkpoint arrest, DNA repair, and apoptosis. ATM activates TP53 via CHK2-mediated phosphorylation, linking DNA damage to tumour suppression. Germline loss-of-function mutations in ATM cause ataxia-telangiectasia, a recessive disorder characterised by progressive cerebellar ataxia, immunodeficiency, radiation sensitivity, and markedly elevated cancer risk. Heterozygous ATM variants moderately increase breast and pancreatic cancer risk and are actionable in some contexts (PARP inhibitor sensitivity). Biallelic ATM loss in tumours causes genomic instability and is associated with poor prognosis in some cancer types.

MDM2 (mouse double minute 2 homolog, UniProt Q00987) is an E3 ubiquitin ligase and the principal negative regulator of TP53. MDM2 binds the transactivation domain of TP53, inhibiting its transcriptional activity and targeting it for proteasomal degradation. The MDM2-TP53 interaction forms a negative feedback loop: TP53 transcriptionally activates MDM2, which in turn suppresses TP53. MDM2 also has TP53-independent oncogenic functions, including regulation of the cell cycle and DNA repair. MDM2 amplification or overexpression occurs in many sarcomas and other tumour types that retain wild-type TP53, effectively neutralising p53 tumour suppression without mutation. MDM2 is a therapeutic target: small molecule inhibitors (nutlins, such as idasanutlin and RG7388) disrupt the MDM2-TP53 interaction, reactivating p53 in TP53 wild-type tumours. MDM4 (MDMX) acts similarly to MDM2 and can cooperate with it to suppress TP53.

RB1 (retinoblastoma protein, UniProt P06400) was the first tumour suppressor identified and encodes the retinoblastoma protein (pRb). pRb regulates the G1-to-S cell cycle transition by binding and inhibiting E2F transcription factors, which are required for expression of genes needed for S-phase entry. Mitogenic signals activate CDK4/6-cyclin D complexes that phosphorylate and inactivate pRb, releasing E2F and permitting S-phase entry. RB1 loss-of-function allows unconstrained E2F activity and uncontrolled cell proliferation. Germline RB1 mutations cause hereditary retinoblastoma — children who inherit one mutant allele develop bilateral retinoblastoma when the second allele is lost somatically (Knudson's two-hit hypothesis). Somatic RB1 inactivation is common in many adult cancers including small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer, and osteosarcoma. CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib) restore RB1 activity indirectly by blocking CDK4/6-mediated pRb inactivation.

PALB2 (partner and localiser of BRCA2, UniProt Q86YC2) encodes a protein that bridges BRCA1 and BRCA2 in the nucleus, enabling efficient homologous recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks. PALB2 binds BRCA1 at its N-terminal coiled-coil domain and BRCA2 at its C-terminal WD40 repeat domain. Loss of PALB2 disrupts the BRCA1-PALB2-BRCA2 complex and impairs RAD51 loading at DNA breaks. Germline pathogenic variants in PALB2 confer a lifetime breast cancer risk of approximately 35-60%, comparable to BRCA2, and also elevate ovarian and pancreatic cancer risk. PALB2 is considered a high-penetrance breast cancer susceptibility gene and is included in clinical gene panels. Biallelic PALB2 mutations cause Fanconi anaemia complementation group N. PALB2-deficient tumours are sensitive to PARP inhibitors, similar to BRCA1/2-deficient tumours. PALB2 frequently co-appears in publications with BRCA1 and BRCA2 due to their shared pathway role.

SciLifeLab (Science for Life Laboratory) is a national centre for molecular biosciences in Sweden, operated jointly by Karolinska Institutet, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm University, and Uppsala University. It provides large-scale research infrastructure including genomics, proteomics, bioinformatics, and imaging platforms to the Swedish and international research community. SciLifeLab Data Centre manages national data infrastructure for life science data, including compute resources, storage, and data management services. The Data Centre operates the Swedish COVID-19 Data Portal and contributes to ELIXIR, the European infrastructure for life science data. SciLifeLab's national genomics platform performs whole-genome sequencing, single-cell RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics at scale. SciLifeLab BioImage Informatics provides training and tools for quantitative image analysis in life science research.
